newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi's Buyoya eases control, many sceptical.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya eases control, many sceptical.

text.p: Burundi's Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya lifted bans on political parties and parliament on Friday but rebels and politicians saw the move as a bid to ease sanctions.
The Tutsi-dominated Burundian army meanwhile said its troops killed seven Hutu rebels on Thursday from a group that had killed Burundi's senior Roman Catholic prelate in an ambush on Monday.

In a statement, Buyoya issued a decree restoring the national assembly and dropping a ban on political parties imposed when he seized power in an army coup on July 25. Neighbouring countries had imposed economic sanctions in response.
"We want a national assembly to help make peace and help negotiate," Buyoya told a news conference, trying to appeal to the African states that imposed sanctions on July 31 until Burundi talks peace.
But he added: "There are conditions for talking to rebels... I don't think you can have dialogue without conditions..."

"The government of Burundi is ready to make peace but if others are ready to make war then we will make war, but a war to bring peace," said the retired army major, who has had little international success since taking power.
The constitution remained suspended and demonstrations banned.

If genuine, the changes meet two of three conditions set by regional leaders for lifting the embargo. The third condition is unconditional peace talks among all Burundi's parties, including Hutu rebels.
"This is a good step, but really it is not enough," said Jerome Ndiho, spokesman for the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), political wing of the main rebel group.
"It cannot be effective until the security of the politicians can be guaranteed, and that can only happen when the army becomes truly national," Ndiho said in Brussels.
Other CNDD officials said the moves were a bid by Buyoya to win an easing of sanctions.
Charles Mukasi, leader of the Tutsi-dominated Uprona party, said parliament had no real power even before the coup but he welcomed the change on political parties.

"Lifting the ban on parliament is a cosmetic change simply designed to please (Julius) Nyerere," Mukasi told Reuters. The former Tanzanian president is the main mediator on Burundi and master-minded sanctions.
"They are restoring an institution that was incapable of functioning. Power is held by the government," added Mukasi.
In Nairobi, a spokesman for exiled members of the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party said the changes amounted to nothing.
An army spokesman said on Friday 50 soldiers clashed on Thursday with rebels at Gitongo, where Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna and two nuns were killed in an ambush on Monday.
"The rebels who attacked the soldiers are the same ones who killed the archbishop," said Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi, adding there were no army casualties.
Four people with the archbishop survived the attack. A Burundian nun killed in the attack was buried on Wednesday but the bodies of Ruhuna and another nun have not been recovered.
